problem: Diffusion-based visual navigation policies (e.g., NoMaD) denoise from Gaussian noise, which is far from the sparse target action distribution. This wastes denoising steps, raises learning difficulty, and gives no guidance toward accurate actions.
motivation: Local planners for image-goal navigation need fast, accurate multimodal action generation on-board robots. Diffusion bridge models can start from an arbitrary informative source distribution, but they need paired data, and imitation learning has no natural source for each target action. The paper builds one from observations and studies how source quality affects the result.
key_idea: Replace Gaussian noise with an observation-conditioned prior action (Gaussian, rule-based parabolic, or CVAE-learned) as the start of a denoising diffusion bridge (DDBM) that generates the target navigation action sequence.
insight: A theoretical error bound says denoising error grows with the KL divergence between source and target distributions, and a 2D toy experiment (Fig. 3) shows the same trend. Table 3 shows that prior-only navigation succeeds rarely (0/8/20%), but the bridge lifts success to 64/44/88%, so the bridge repairs weak priors and better priors help more. Fig. 5 and Table 2 show that DDBM stays stable as steps drop to 1-4 while DDPM degrades. A poorly designed rule-based prior can hurt, e.g. indoor basic success falls to 62% against NoMaD's 86%.
method: Feature extraction: an EfficientNet/Transformer encoder over past RGB observations and a goal image produces the context vector c_t.
Prior action generation: three options give the source action a_T from c_t: Gaussian noise, a rule-based prior, or a learning-based CVAE prior.

Rule-based prior: an FC layer predicts path length and one of 5 movement classes (straight, left, right, U-turn left, U-turn right). A parabola through the origin and the endpoint is sampled at evenly spaced points, with confidence-scaled noise added.
Learning-based prior: a lightweight CVAE conditioned on observations, trained with an MSE + KL loss, gives the source action.

Diffusion bridge denoiser: a 1D temporal CNN with FiLM conditioning on c_t, using a DDBM VE bridge (sigma0=sigmaT=0.5) with EDM preconditioning, predicts a_0 from (a_t, a_T, t). The default is k=10 denoising steps.
Training loss: L = λb·Lb (weighted bridge MSE) + λp·Lp (prior loss: MSE+CE for rule-based, MSE+KL for CVAE) + λd·Ld (temporal distance loss, following NoMaD).

setting.backbone: NaviBridger: Transformer encoder + FiLM-conditioned 1D-CNN DDBM denoiser + prior module (FC or CVAE), trained from scratch
setting.training_data: Real-world public navigation datasets as in NoMaD: RECON, SCAND, GoStanford, SACSoN. Some tests fine-tune on limited simulation trajectories. 30 epochs, lr 1e-4, batch 256 (224 for learning-based), about 30 h on one RTX TITAN.
setting.observation: monocular RGB observation history + goal image
setting.action_space: predicted waypoint sequence (local path) tracked by the robot, topological-map subgoal images from a high-level planner
setting.simulator: Gazebo (Stanford 2D-3D-S indoor, Gazebo CitySim outdoor) with Jackal robot; real world with Diablo robot
setting.privileged: none (a topological map of goal images is used by the high-level planner)

numbers_note: Only the authors' own custom simulation tasks are reported (no standard benchmark). The full Table 1 has 3 own variants x 2 scenes x 2 tasks; only the main variant is fully listed, plus Gaussian and rule-based for the indoor adaptation task. Success rates in Fig. 5 (e.g. about 90% at 10 steps) appear only in a figure. Sample sizes are not stated.
results: The learning-based prior gives the best results in all four simulated tasks: indoor 92%/88% success and outdoor 44%/64%. It beats NoMaD (86/32 indoor, 22/52 outdoor) and ViNT, with fewer collisions. The bridge stays stable with 1-4 denoising steps where DDPM degrades, and it works in real-world deployment on a Diablo robot.
limitations: Evaluation uses only custom, small-scale simulation tasks and qualitative real-world demos, with no standard benchmark or numeric real-world results.
The rule-based prior is hand-designed and can hurt performance (indoor basic success 62% vs NoMaD's 86%). At equal step counts DDBM inference is slower than DDPM.
Fast-moving dynamic obstacles are not handled.
